content: 1. Dicofol is a chemical that can be found in water, and its exposure through food varies significantly depending on local conditions and its usage. It has been proposed as a persistent organic pollutant under the Stockholm Convention. 2. In an acute neurotoxicity study conducted on rats, a No-Observed-Adverse-Effect Level (NOAEL) of 15 mg/kg body weight was identified for effects such as reduced body weight and decreased feed intake. A safety factor of 100 was applied, resulting in a derived value of 2 mg/kg body weight. 3. The detection of dicofol in water can be effectively achieved using solvent extraction followed by gas chromatography with electron capture detection (GC-ECD), with a quantification limit of 5 ng/L. 4. Dicofol can be removed from water through adsorption onto activated carbon. Additionally, any dicofol adsorbed onto particulate matter is likely to be removed during the coagulation process in water treatment. 5. A health-based value for dicofol in drinking water has been derived, allocating 20% of the upper bound of the Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) for a 60 kg adult consuming 2 liters of water per day. For acute exposure, 100% of the Acute Reference Dose (ARfD) is allocated under the same conditions. 6. Dicofol exposure primarily affects body weight and feed intake in experimental animals, with increased liver weight and changes in liver enzyme activities observed. Liver tumors were noted in male mice at doses associated with significant enzyme induction and liver hypertrophy. However, due to the absence of genotoxicity and carcinogenic effects in rats, dicofol is unlikely to pose a carcinogenic risk to humans at anticipated dietary exposure levels. 7. The margin of safety between the upper bound of the ADI and the Lowest-Observed-Adverse-Effect Level (LOAEL) for liver adenomas in male mice is approximately 20,000. 8. Diquat is a non-selective, fast-acting contact herbicide used for weed control in food crops, residential areas, and aquatic environments. It is highly water-soluble but strongly adsorbed to soil, making it resistant to degradation in the sorbed state. Photochemical degradation occurs in the presence of sunlight. 9. Food exposure to diquat is generally low. The default allocation factor of 20% accounts for the fact that available food exposure data, which suggest low exposure, do not typically include information from developing countries where exposure may be higher. 10. Diquat primarily targets the eyes following short-term repeated exposure in rats and dogs. Effects on the kidneys, liver, and hematological parameters have also been observed. It is not carcinogenic in mice or rats and does not cause reproductive or developmental toxicity in animal studies. 11. Lead exposure is associated with a wide range of health effects, including neurodevelopmental impairments, cardiovascular mortality, renal dysfunction, hypertension, reduced fertility, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Neurodevelopmental effects in children occur at lower blood lead concentrations than other effects and are the most consistent across studies. 12. Lead in drinking water primarily arises from the corrosion of household plumbing systems containing lead pipes, solder, or fittings. Factors such as pH, temperature, alkalinity, and water standing time influence the amount of lead dissolved. 13. The guideline value for lead in drinking water is set at 10 µg/L, designated as provisional due to treatment performance and analytical limitations. Efforts to reduce lead exposure from all sources, including drinking water, are emphasized. 14. Infants and children are the most sensitive subgroups to lead exposure. Measures to reduce lead contamination include removing lead-containing plumbing and fittings, using lead-free materials in new installations, and implementing corrosion control. 15. Sampling protocols for lead in water depend on the objective. First-draw samples typically show the highest lead concentrations, while flushed samples provide consistent values. Random daytime samples reflect consumer exposure but require more samples to determine mean levels. 16. The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) concluded that the Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intake (PTWI) for lead could no longer be considered health-protective and was withdrawn. It is not possible to establish a new PTWI due to the lack of a threshold for key effects. 17. Lead is exceptional among chemical hazards in drinking water because most lead arises from plumbing and service connections. Addressing this issue requires significant time and financial investment, emphasizing the need for practical measures to reduce total lead exposure.
